meta.lessonLength: 45-minute core; shorten guided practice/game application for shorter periods or add a second round for longer periods
meta.safetyNote: Teacher judgment, student needs, facility conditions, and school policy override any generic activity suggestion.

Week 1.answer: Routines help everyone know where to go, what to do, when to stop, and how to use equipment safely.
Week 1.objective: Students will practice entry, exit, attention signal, and safe freeze. Success is shown when they apply at least two teaching cues during “Entry/exit practice; freeze signal” and complete the routine checklist.
Week 1.opening: 4 minutes — Meet at home spots, read the question aloud, and invite a quick prediction or movement response. State the student-friendly answer, review boundaries and the stop signal, then warm up: Practice entering, finding home base, freezing on the signal, and moving safely to two different locations.
Week 1.skillInstruction: 8 minutes — Mark home spots, boundaries, equipment homes, and one clear entry/exit route before students arrive. Name and demonstrate the weekly focus: Practice entry, exit, attention signal, and safe freeze. Model a successful example and one common error. Ask students to identify the difference, then rehearse the first two cues at half speed.
Week 1.guidedPractice: 12 minutes — Rehearse each routine separately: enter, find home base, respond to the stop signal, move inside boundaries, collect one item, return it, and exit. Reset immediately and repeat until the class can complete the sequence safely with fewer reminders. Circulate using one concise feedback cycle: name what worked, give one next cue, and watch the retry.
Week 1.gameApplication: 16 minutes — Run three short movement rounds. Between rounds, change one condition such as equipment, grouping, or location so students must apply the same routine instead of merely memorizing one path. End each round with a rapid freeze-and-reset check. Pause midway for water and a 45-second question check, then let students apply one adjustment in the final round.
Week 1.closure: 5 minutes — Return equipment, cool down, and revisit “How do routines help everyone learn and move safely?” Students answer with one claim and one example from today. Preview the next lesson or name one safe way to practice the skill outside class.
cues: Freeze: feet still, equipment still, eyes on teacher
Move only inside the marked boundary
Week 1.assessment: Routine checklist. Use three look-fors: Start at home base; Freeze: feet still, equipment still, eyes on teacher; Move only inside the marked boundary. Mark each student Ready, Developing, or Not Yet and note one reteach group for the next class.
adaptations: Support: reduce distance, speed, repetitions, or decision load; use a larger/lighter object and repeat one cue at a time.
Access: pair verbal directions with a visual signal or picture cue; offer standing, seated, rolling, or upper-body participation when it meets the same learning target.
Challenge: increase distance, add a direction or non-dominant-side choice, or ask the student to explain and apply a strategy.
Sensory access: provide visual counts/signals and allow reduced sound or a quieter practice space.
K–2 pacing: use short rounds, concrete demonstrations, picture boundaries, and frequent successful resets.
safety: Inspect the floor, boundaries, and equipment before class; keep exits and water access clear.
Use a visual and verbal stop signal. Students freeze with equipment still before directions or retrieval.

Pause midway for water and a 45-second question check, then let students apply one adjustment in the final round.

Pause midway for water and a 45-second question check, then let students apply one adjustment in the final round.

Week 14.gameApplication: 16 minutes — Use a progression ladder: beat jumps, single swing-and-jump, consecutive jumps, then a partner or long-rope challenge. Students choose the level that keeps technique safe. Require students to explain the choice or strategy that improved the result. Week 14.closure: 5 minutes — Return equipment, cool down, and revisit “How can rhythm improve movement?” Students answer with one claim and one example from today. Preview the next lesson or name one safe way to practice the skill outside class.

Circulate using one concise feedback cycle: name what worked, give one next cue, and watch the retry.
Week 15.gameApplication: 16 minutes — Students perform or design a short sequence, then use one success criterion to give partner feedback. Emphasize control over difficult tricks. Week 15.assessment: Sequence rubric. Use three look-fors: Still eyes; Strong base; Soft knees. Mark each student Ready, Developing, or Not Yet and note one reteach group for the next class.

Week 24.answer: Accuracy depends on alignment and a repeatable release; force must match distance, object, and target size. More force does not help if control is lost.
Week 24.objective: Students will adjust force and direction for target accuracy. Success is shown when they apply at least three teaching cues during “Kings Kone target strategy with foam-ball rules” and complete the accuracy record.
Week 24.opening: 4 minutes — Meet at home spots, read the question aloud, and invite a quick prediction or movement response. State the student-friendly answer, review boundaries and the stop signal, then warm up: Shadow the day’s skill without equipment, then move to open space on visual cues.

Name and demonstrate the weekly focus: Adjust force and direction for target accuracy. Model a successful example and one common error. Ask students to identify the difference, then rehearse the first two cues at half speed.
Week 24.guidedPractice: 12 minutes — Teach side-to-target throwing, controlled force, and aiming below shoulder height at cones only. Students may retrieve balls on their own side but may not cross the center line, guard directly in front of a cone, or throw at people. Circulate using one concise feedback cycle: name what worked, give one next cue, and watch the retry.
Week 24.gameApplication: 16 minutes — Teams score by knocking over target cones, then reset them between short rounds. Everyone remains active; there is no player elimination. Change distance or cone size to balance success. Require students to explain the choice or strategy that improved the result. Pause midway for water and a 45-second question check, then let students apply one adjustment in the final round.
Week 24.closure: 5 minutes — Return equipment, cool down, and revisit “How do force and accuracy affect a target result?” Students answer with one claim and one example from today. Preview the next lesson or name one safe way to practice the skill outside class.
